subject: history
subtitle: The transatlantic slave trade, the lived experience of enslaved people, and the abolition movement.

data.targetWord: the forced transportation and sale of millions of African people across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas, mainly between the 1500s and 1800s

examples.en-GB: Britain became one of the largest slave-trading nations during the height of the transatlantic slave trade.

data.targetWord: the forced sea journey of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic Ocean from Africa to the Americas, often in dangerous and dehumanising conditions

examples.en-GB: Many enslaved people died during the Middle Passage from disease, violence, hunger and despair.

data.targetWord: a simplified model describing the trade routes between Europe, Africa and the Americas, in which manufactured goods went to Africa, enslaved people were transported to the Americas, and plantation products were brought back to Europe

examples.en-GB: Triangular trade shows how the slave system connected three continents for the profit of European merchants.

data.targetWord: a large farm in the Americas that grew one main cash crop such as sugar, cotton or tobacco, using enslaved labour to maximise profit

examples.en-GB: Sugar plantations in the Caribbean depended entirely on the forced labour of enslaved Africans.

data.targetWord: a system in which people are legally treated as property that can be bought, sold and inherited, with no rights of their own

examples.en-GB: Under chattel slavery, colonial laws treated enslaved people as property rather than as human beings.

data.targetWord: action taken against control or oppression, which could be large or small, public or hidden; enslaved people resisted in many ways including everyday sabotage, escape and organised revolt

examples.en-GB: Resistance by enslaved people, from breaking tools to organising rebellions, was central to weakening the slave system.

data.targetWord: the legal ending of a system, especially the ending of the slave trade (1807) and later of slavery itself in most British colonies (1833)

examples.en-GB: The abolition of the slave trade in 1807 made it illegal for British ships to transport enslaved Africans, but did not free those already enslaved.

data.targetWord: a person who campaigned actively to end the slave trade or slavery, including both Black and white campaigners in Britain and the Americas

examples.en-GB: Olaudah Equiano was an influential abolitionist whose autobiography gave British readers powerful testimony against the slave trade.

data.targetWord: evidence given by someone describing their own direct experience; the written and spoken accounts of formerly enslaved people were powerful tools in the abolition campaign

examples.en-GB: Mary Prince's testimony, published in 1831, exposed the continuing violence of slavery in British colonies.

data.targetWord: refusing to buy or use something as a form of protest; abolitionists encouraged consumers to boycott slave-grown sugar to put pressure on the plantation economy

examples.en-GB: The sugar boycott campaign asked British households to refuse slave-grown sugar as a way of protesting against the slave trade.

data.targetWord: the successful revolution beginning in 1791 in Saint-Domingue (now Haiti) in which enslaved people fought against slavery and colonial rule, resulting in Haitian independence in 1804

examples.en-GB: The Haitian Revolution proved that enslaved people could successfully overthrow slavery and colonial rule, alarming enslavers across the Atlantic world.

data.targetWord: money paid as a remedy for loss; after the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act, £20 million was paid to enslavers, while enslaved people received nothing

examples.en-GB: The unfair compensation settlement of 1833 paid enslavers for their so-called 'property' but gave formerly enslaved people no payment for their stolen lives and labour.

data.targetWord: the system imposed after 1834 in which formerly enslaved people were forced to continue working for their former enslavers for a period before gaining full freedom

examples.en-GB: The apprenticeship system delayed full freedom for many formerly enslaved people until 1838.

data.targetWord: the ability of people to make choices and take action, even in very difficult circumstances; historians emphasise the agency of enslaved people to challenge the view that they were merely passive victims

examples.en-GB: Historians now emphasise the agency of enslaved people, recognising their active resistance, cultural survival and campaigning.

data.targetWord: the long-term impact of an event, system or decision on later generations and society; the legacy of transatlantic slavery includes ongoing racism, wealth inequalities and cultural survival

examples.en-GB: The legacy of transatlantic slavery continues to shape debates about reparations, memorials, and racial inequality in Britain and elsewhere.

data.targetWord: an English trading company chartered in 1672 that organised trade in enslaved Africans and goods from West Africa, showing state involvement in the slave trade

examples.en-GB: The Royal African Company had a monopoly on the English slave trade until 1698, after which other merchants also became involved.

data.targetWord: an African writer and abolitionist whose 1789 autobiography described his life, enslavement and freedom, becoming one of the most powerful pieces of evidence against the slave trade

examples.en-GB: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography helped British readers understand the cruelty of the slave trade from a first-hand perspective.

data.targetWord: the 1781 incident in which enslaved Africans were thrown overboard from the slave ship Zong so that the owners could claim insurance, which helped expose the brutality of the trade to British campaigners

examples.en-GB: The Zong massacre of 1781 shocked many people in Britain and strengthened the case of abolitionists.

data.targetWord: communities of people spread away from their original homeland, often through forced movement; the African diaspora resulted from the transatlantic slave trade

examples.en-GB: The African diaspora created by the slave trade has shaped cultures across the Caribbean, the Americas and Britain.

data.targetWord: an economic system based on large farms growing cash crops using enslaved labour, connected to trade networks across the Atlantic that enriched merchants, ports and industries in Europe

examples.en-GB: The plantation economy linked Caribbean sugar producers directly to British cities such as Liverpool, Bristol and London.

data.targetWord: ideas, systems or actions that treat people unfairly or as inferior based on their race or ethnicity; racist ideas were developed and used by Europeans to justify enslaving African people

examples.en-GB: Racist ideas claiming African people were inferior were used to try to justify the slave trade, but these ideas were false.

data.targetWord: a British abolitionist who collected evidence against the slave trade including diagrams, objects and testimonies, providing campaigners with powerful material for speeches and publications

examples.en-GB: Thomas Clarkson travelled Britain gathering evidence and supporters for the abolition campaign.

data.targetWord: the British law that abolished slavery in most British colonies, coming into effect in 1834, though formerly enslaved people were forced into apprenticeship until 1838 and enslavers received £20 million in compensation

examples.en-GB: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833 ended legal slavery in most British colonies but compensated enslavers rather than enslaved people.

data.targetWord: the preservation by enslaved people of their languages, music, religion, food, stories and family practices as a form of identity and resistance against a system designed to dehumanise them

examples.en-GB: Cultural survival was a vital form of resistance because it protected the humanity, identity and community of enslaved people.

data.targetWord: a group of lands or peoples controlled by one country or ruler; European empires, including the British Empire, created the plantation system that drove demand for enslaved African labour

examples.en-GB: The British Empire's expansion in the Caribbean and Americas increased demand for enslaved people to work on plantations.

data.title: Put the key events in the history of transatlantic slavery and abolition in chronological order
items: Portuguese traders begin buying enslaved Africans on the West African coast (1440s)
John Hawkins makes an English slaving voyage (1562)
Royal African Company is chartered to organise English slave trade (1672)
Zong massacre exposes brutality to British campaigners (1781)
Abolitionist society formed in Britain (1787)
Equiano's autobiography published (1789)
Haitian Revolution begins (1791)
Britain abolishes the slave trade (1807)
Slavery Abolition Act passed (1833)
Apprenticeship ends in British Caribbean colonies (1838)

data.title: Order the stages of triangular trade from Europe
items: European ships carry manufactured goods (textiles, guns, metal goods) to West Africa
Enslaved Africans are purchased or captured at coastal trading posts in Africa
Enslaved people are transported across the Atlantic on the Middle Passage
Enslaved people arrive in the Americas and are sold at auction
Enslaved people work on plantations growing sugar, tobacco or cotton
Plantation goods are shipped back to European ports
Merchants in cities like Liverpool, Bristol and London profit from the trade

data.title: Order the different types of resistance by enslaved people from small-scale to large-scale
items: Slowing down work and pretending not to understand orders
Breaking tools and hiding food for families
Preserving cultural practices, songs, languages and beliefs
Escaping temporarily or permanently from the plantation
Petitioning courts and publishing written testimony
Organising local revolts against plantation owners
Large-scale rebellions such as the Jamaica Baptist War of 1831
The Haitian Revolution, which destroyed slavery in a major colony
